issues.legal_issue: The circumstantial evidence, with the confession excluded, was insufficient to sustain the conviction because it did not exclude reasonable alternative explanations.
material_facts: The case against the accused, apart from the excluded confession, rested on his motive, a lie about the deceased’s movements, and his knowledge of the murder and the concealment of the body and belongings thirteen days later.
Other members of the accused’s family shared the motive and had similar opportunities to commit the crime.
The accused’s brother was also suspected, had absconded, and could have been the source of the accused’s later knowledge.
The evidence did not show that the accused was with the deceased when the deceased was last seen.
issues.conclusion: The circumstances did not establish the accused’s guilt; the conviction was set aside and the accused was acquitted.
issues.legal_principle: A circumstantial case must support the conclusion of guilt rather than leave reasonable alternative hypotheses unexcluded. Here, the circumstances relied on could point with equal suspicion to other family members, so they did not sustain the conviction. The confession was excluded for the separate reason that the accused had not been questioned about it under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.circumstantial_case: The prosecution relies on circumstantial evidence rather than direct evidence of the accused committing the crime.
predicates.other_suspects_shared_motive_and_opportu: Other possible suspects shared the accused’s motive and had similar opportunities to commit the crime.
predicates.reasonable_alternative_explanations_rema: The evidence leaves reasonable explanations of the crime that do not establish the accused’s guilt.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal challenges a conviction based on circumstantial evidence and reasonable alternatives remain, the conviction is set aside and an acquittal is ordered.

issues.legal_issue: A confession should not be relied on when the accused was not fairly questioned about it and the circumstances leave the accused without a fair opportunity to explain it.
material_facts: The accused made a confession after discoveries had already been made following his arrest.
The accused was not questioned about the confession under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
The confession was made eight days after the arrest, during which much might have happened, and the accused’s account of that interval had not been obtained.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in excluding the confession from the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 imposes a duty on the court to question the accused fairly and properly, in clear and simple language, about the case and each material point against him, so that he has an opportunity to explain. In the circumstances here, the failure to question the accused about the confession left its reliability and the possible prejudice from relying on it unresolved; the High Court was justified in excluding it. No earlier case is identified by name in the supplied judgment as authority for this ruling.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which a confession is offered against the accused.
predicates.accused_not_questioned_about_confession: The trial court did not question the accused about the confession or give the accused an opportunity to explain it.
predicates.confession_made_after_material_interveni: The confession was made after an interval in which significant events occurred that could bear on the accused’s account or the confession’s reliability.

issues.definition: In a criminal trial, when the accused was not questioned about a confession and material events intervened before it was made, the confession is excluded from evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A retrial should not be ordered to cure a material failure to examine the accused when the failure is not merely technical and a retrial would prolong the accused’s harassment after an already lengthy trial.
material_facts: The accused had been on trial for more than four and a half years.
The trial court had not questioned the accused about the confession as required by section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
The failure was not a mere technicality, and the prosecution sought to reopen the matter and, if necessary, have the case remanded.
The evidence remaining after exclusion of the confession did not sustain the conviction.
issues.conclusion: The Court refused a retrial, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the accused.
issues.legal_principle: A court must balance the duty to ensure that the guilty do not escape against the accused’s right to a fair trial and protection from indefinite harassment. Where a trial court’s material failure is not merely technical, a retrial should not be ordered merely to repair its consequences, particularly after prolonged proceedings and where the remaining evidence does not sustain guilt. The judgment states that it is not laying down a general rule for all cases. It applies section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 and identifies no earlier case by name as authority for the refusal to remand.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_in_which_retrial_is_sought and prolonged_proceedings and material_trial_court_failure and failure_not_merely_technical and remaining_evidence_does_not_sustain_conviction

predicates.criminal_appeal_in_which_retrial_is_soug: The proceeding is a criminal appeal in which a party seeks a retrial or remand.
predicates.prolonged_proceedings: The accused has already been subject to lengthy criminal proceedings.
predicates.material_trial_court_failure: The trial court failed to perform a duty that materially affected the fairness or reliability of the trial.
predicates.failure_not_merely_technical: The trial court’s failure is substantive rather than a harmless procedural irregularity.
predicates.remaining_evidence_does_not_sustain_conv: After the evidence affected by the trial court’s failure is excluded, the remaining evidence does not establish guilt.

issues.definition: When a retrial is sought after prolonged proceedings, a material non-technical trial court failure, and insufficient remaining evidence, retrial is refused and an acquittal is ordered.
